performers: Johanna Gadski, soprano; Frank La Forge, piano
intro: One Victor side holds two songs, and Beach’s Browning setting is the second. Johanna Gadski sings it after a song by her accompanist Frank La Forge, on a disc cut in January 1908.

B′ · The opening lines return and climb

cues.title: Two songs on one disc side
cues.text: The label of Victor 87026 lists both songs on one side: La Forge’s first, Beach’s second. Gadski sings with La Forge at the piano; the take was made on 14 January 1908.
cues.evidence: The Victor 87026 label, photographed for the Library of Congress National Jukebox, reads “(a) How Much I Love You (La Forge) (b) The Year’s at the Spring (Beach)”. The Discography of American Historical Recordings dates matrix B-5018, take 2, to 14 January 1908. https://archive.org/download/loc-jukebox-125920-how-much-i-love-you/jukebox-125920_label.jpg https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/200006832

cues.title: Beach’s Browning setting
cues.text: After a pause the Beach song begins, the first of her three Browning songs, Op. 44. A. P. Schmidt published them in 1900, dedicated to the Browning Society of Boston. The piano repeats chords under the voice.
cues.evidence: A. P. Schmidt’s first edition of 1900 carries the dedication “To the Browning Society of Boston” and marks the song Allegro di molto; its piano part is built on repeated chords. https://archive.org/details/per_women-composers-collection_the-years-at-the-spring_1900
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening lines come round again
cues.text: After “dew-pearled” the music slows, then Beach starts over at tempo, so “The year’s at the spring” is sung twice before the lark, the snail and “God’s in his heaven”. The song ends on “All’s right with the world”.
cues.evidence: In the 1900 edition, pages 3–5, the voice slows with a poco rall. and rit. at “dew-pearled”, resumes a tempo with the opening lines, and then sets the lark, the snail and “God’s in his heaven” before “All’s right with the world”. https://archive.org/details/per_women-composers-collection_the-years-at-the-spring_1900
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.background:
Amy Marcy Cheney was born on 5 September 1867 in Henniker, New Hampshire, the only child of a paper manufacturer and a singer-pianist. At four she spent a summer on her grandfather’s farm in West Henniker, where there was no piano, and composed three waltzes in her head; she played them when she got home. Her mother would not teach her the piano until she was six. “I was not allowed to climb up on her lap, or on the music stool,” Beach remembered. “I could only hear music, think music.”

The Cheneys moved to Chelsea, Massachusetts, in 1871 and to Boston in 1875. Ernst Perabo and then Carl Baermann, a pupil of Liszt, taught her the piano; Junius Hill gave her a year of harmony. Boston musicians told her parents to send her to Europe. They kept her at home. On 24 October 1883, aged sixteen, she played Moscheles’s G minor Concerto and Chopin’s E♭ Rondo at the Boston Music Hall. Her first song in print, The Rainy Day, a Longfellow setting, appeared the same year. On 28 March 1885 she played Chopin’s F minor Concerto with the Boston Symphony under Wilhelm Gericke.
